source.title: Alignment via Training Against Probes Without Losing Monitorability
source.authors: Lena Libon; Alexander Panfilov; Ben Rank; Xin Chen; Jonas Geiping; Maksym Andriushchenko

record.file_problem: The text includes some garbled figure text, but the relevant methods and Table 8 results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies Heretic abliteration to model checkpoints and measures harmfulness before and after the edit. This tests practical refusal-direction removal, but not the original difference-in-means projection procedure.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are Table 8's before/after Heretic abliteration scores on ClearHarm. The study does not itself find a difference-in-means direction, project it out at every layer and position, or add it to induce refusal. Its other probe-training, utility, and safety results do not test those operations. Claims about methods from cited work are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The study applies Heretic abliteration, a search-based variant of directional ablation rather than the original difference-in-means projection, to a released model, Llama 3 8B Instruct. Harmfulness rises from 0.09 to 0.76, which bears on V2. The other Table 8 rows abliterate checkpoints whose safety came from probe training, not refusal training. Explicit refusals are at most 1% in these checkpoints, so those rows measure a related but different construct and do not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right and should be extended. The authors conclude that continuously updated probe-trained checkpoints resist Heretic abliteration (changes of −0.03 to +0.07, versus +0.67 for Llama 3 8B Instruct). They attribute this to the method not relying on refusal demonstrations. Retrained checkpoints resist less consistently, and frozen ones were already unsafe. The authors also report that this safety does not survive later LoRA fine-tuning, even on benign data only, and that their non-adaptive attacks cannot establish security.
record.recipe_differences: The original method identifies a difference-in-means activation direction and projects it out; this study applies Heretic abliteration, which searches over shared and layer-specific directions and edits selected checkpoints. It is a different practical weight-edit procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect differs by checkpoint and training regime. Heretic searches over shared and layer-specific directions for 200 Optuna trials and selects the trial with the fewest refusals at KL ≤ 1.

fits_no_version.finding: Heretic abliteration barely changes harmfulness in checkpoints made safe by continuously updated probe training (−0.03 to +0.07). The same attack raises retrained checkpoints by up to +0.22. These models rarely refuse; they soft-refuse, pseudo-comply or produce disrupted text. Benign-only LoRA fine-tuning later removes this safety (e.g. 0.09 to 0.83).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety instilled without refusal demonstrations, by training against harmfulness probes, is not carried by a removable refusal direction, so refusal-direction abliteration does not undo it.

record.code_released: not stated (the text names aisa-group/training against probes)
record.problems: The abliteration comparison uses 40 ClearHarm prompts and DeepSeek v4 Flash as the judge; Table 8 reports no uncertainty. The authors caution that their attack evaluation does not establish model security. Utility is evaluated for the trained checkpoints, but not reported after the Table 8 abliteration edits.
record.rows_left_out: None of the Table 8 before/after results were left out. Other probe-training and utility results were not extracted because they do not measure removal of the refusal direction.

untested.parts: Difference-in-means direction, projection at every layer and position, inducing refusal by activation addition.
Original difference-in-means weight edit; any released model other than Llama 3 8B Instruct; refusal rate as such, since harmfulness is measured instead.
Whether jailbreaks act by suppressing the direction; training against the direction's ablation. Probe-guided training is not ablation-adversarial training.
All. The probe polytopes are detectors of harmfulness, not descriptions of how refusal is encoded.
All, for refusal training specifically. See fits_no_version for the related finding on non-refusal safety training.

missing.what: Llama 3 8B Instruct before and after Heretic abliteration (the abliterated base). StrongREJECT: direct query 0.09→0.76, GCG 0.10→0.34, prefill 0.59→0.72. Utility: MMLU 0.62→0.61, GSM8K 0.52→0.50, IFEval 0.52→0.58.
XSTest over-refusal on safe prompts: Llama 3 8B Instruct 0.03 vs abliterated base 0.01.
Qualitative example: Llama 3 8B Instruct refuses a bomb tutorial request; its abliterated variant complies.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The only row testing V2 is a single reference model evaluated on 40 prompts with an LLM judge and no uncertainty reported. Heretic searches over shared and layer-specific directions for 200 Optuna trials under a KL ≤ 1 constraint, so it differs from the original difference-in-means procedure. The record's V3 links and labels are dropped because the study does not train against ablation. Probe-trained checkpoints are not refusal-trained models, so their resistance to abliteration does not limit V2; it is recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: The difference-in-means direction, projection at every layer and position, activation addition, and retention of general abilities after those interventions are not tested.
The study tests Heretic abliteration on selected checkpoints, not every released model or every abliteration procedure.

It tests removal of estimated refusal directions and the resulting robustness of probe-trained checkpoints. It does not test training specifically against an ablation attack, or establish that successful attacks work by suppressing this direction.
The probe/polytope comparison concerns training detectors, not whether refusal is encoded by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer of a refusal direction is tested.
The study compares probe-update regimes, not how or when refusal training creates a removable direction.
Qwen3-14B is a reasoning model in the honesty experiments, but the study does not test whether the refusal direction claim holds in reasoning models.

relationships.display_finding: StrongREJECT rose from 0.09 to 0.76, while MMLU, GSM8K and IFEval remained near original performance.
